utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Re begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might I raise the question of the structure of this afternoon's sitting sessions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would it be convenient for the Trial Chamber if we aimed to take the first break between the Prosecution and the Defence responses so that the Defence teams could have an opportunity to discuss time allocation amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's agreeable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that if the last session would be a long session, it would be a bit the other order, that's one hour, one hour and a half, and perhaps even a longer one. Let's keep whether we can keep them relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. Before I give an opportunity to you, Mr. Re, to present further argument in rebuttal for which we have reserved one hour, there's one matter I would like to raise with all parties, and that is that neither in the final brief of the Prosecutor nor in any of the final briefs of the Defence any attention has been paid to mitigating or aggravating circumstances. Now, I fully understand that a Defence which pleads that the Chamber should acquit the accused would not spend much attention on certain mitigating circumstances, which are -- especially if they are crime-related. But of course at the same time in the case law of this Tribunal mitigating circumstances have been accepted which are totally unrelated to the crimes charged, such as, for example, good behaviour in the United Nations Detention Unit. I'm not encouraging you to say that all the accused did behave while in the United Nations Detention Unit because if you see what the weight of this mitigating circumstance is, then one could wonder whether it was ever accepted as such. But of course it's part of the case law of this Tribunal, and I -- I just noticed that there's nothing for the Chamber at this moment to rely upon if considering, which we have to do -- in considering the mitigating or aggravating circumstances. This is just -- yes, personal circumstances, of course, may also play a role in this respect. For example, family composition of most of the accused is even unknown to the Chamber. I'm not urging you to do it, but I just put this on the record. Mr. Re, the same is true, you have of course paid some attention to sentencing but have not in the final brief. I think it was approximately four paragraphs at the end, but no specific reference to any aggravating or mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Our submission is simply it's a joint criminal enterprise. We've set out the role played by each in our brief, and we say that's the appropriate sentence based upon sentencing practices of the Tribunal in their role. I don't propose to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, but of course it's clear that if one of the parties would invoke the existence of mitigating or aggravating circumstances, the Chamber would of course deal with that explicitly in the judgement, and otherwise of course the Chamber will, perhaps, have to consider it anyhow proprio motu. But none of the parties has brought to the attention of this Chamber the existence of any mitigating or aggravating circumstances, and even personal circumstances are not specifically dealt with. Having -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because of the procedural status of which we're in, I offer this as a suggestion. I don't know whether or not the Chamber is amenable to this. I know it did occur in the earlier days, which is, that after a judgement, if need be, we could file at that time briefs with regard to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Rules -- the early set of rules that applied in this Tribunal still had a two-stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- proceedings. That is, first a decision on guilt and then hearings in between and then finally a sentencing decision. That system has been abandoned, and therefore it's one decision. So therefore to say if we could first deliver the judgement in the judgement you find the sentence; that's the new system. So therefore -- of course, if there is a conviction of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's no conviction, there's no sentence either. But that's -- at this moment that's the system. So the Chamber just -- we have still a couple of hours to go. Even if it would be very briefly -- if the parties want to do so, this is the last opportunity to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Re, the Chamber granted one hour for the Prosecution, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are a number of things I'll respond to from the submissions made by counsel for the accused over the last two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first thing I'm going to say is that contrary to Mr. Emmerson's somewhat surprising submission yesterday of there being no direct evidence against the accused, the Prosecution did, in fact, lead strong direct evidence against Haradinaj in Count 3 and 4 regarding the Stojanovics; Balaj, in relation to Witness 4, the rape in Count 36, and Sanije Balaj in Counts 21, 22; and in relation to Lahi Brahimaj strong evidence was led in relation to Witnesses 3, 6, and his involvement with Pal Krasniqi. Now, the case against Haradinaj is circumstantial but it's strong. And in oral submissions, as in his final brief filed, Mr. Emmerson urges you to examine -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- albeit carefully, and of course as you should each piece of evidence. However, the artificial -- artificially constricted approach he urges upon you is quite flawed. This case is, as I don't need to remind you, a mass murder case, and mass murder cases by definition, Your Honours, involve multiple corpses. And when a case is circumstantial, as parts of this case are, you must examine the evidence in its totality. And we, the Prosecution, of course concede that if you were to examine say only one random body found at the canal, a reasonable doubt may of course exist as to, A, the existence of a joint criminal enterprise; or B, the participation of any or all of the accused in it. But that of itself just illustrates the flaw in Mr. Emmerson's approach and urged on you by other Defence counsel because it is only when you put all of the pieces together, as we have in our final trial brief and now in our oral submissions, that the true picture emerges of the extent and the membership of this joint criminal enterprise. And of course Mr. Emmerson is correct when he says the evidence should be looked at in relation to each event individually. We've never suggested otherwise, but what you must do, as you know, is to weigh all of that evidence in its totality to assess whether the circumstances show Haradinaj must have had a hand in those series of killings, the mass murders I referred to a moment ago. And the Prosecution's case is and it's proved it and given all of the circumstances, no reasonable explanation for these crimes exists other than that Haradinaj must have known that at least some of these crimes were being committed by men under his command, that is, men with whom he was working to assert exclusive control of the KLA Dukagjini Zone. But it is, I'll emphasise this again, a case of similarities, of links, of pieces of evidence that have to be assessed in conjunction with each other, of pieces that come together to show where they all fit into the picture, and it's only then that the clear overall pattern emerges. Now, of all the names that -- of the victims that Mr. Emmerson put to you yesterday, saying in effect that the circumstances in each should be carefully considered but in isolation, only two of the 26 identified victims found at the canal in September 1998 do not entirely fit the pattern of targeted Serb civilians, collaborators, and perceived enemies, et cetera, and these two are Afrim Sylejmani and Melush Meha. But my last statement only applies insofar as there is no direct evidence of their abduction or their appearing on a KLA wanted list, but as set out in our brief Afrim Sylejmani was a former state employee, former teacher, which provided motive to the KLA, and Melush Meha lived in a Serbian minority area in Peje which also provided an association with the Serb enemy, colonizer or occupier as the KLA General Staff was describing them. Afrim's body was of course found next to that of Kujtim Imeraj, of whom you heard direct evidence of how he was last -- how he was last seen alive being abducted by KLA members on about the 4th of July, 1998. His body's on the screen at the moment. Melush Meha's body was found by the canal wall directly under the bullet-holes and next to the body of Pal Krasniqi, who you know was last seen alive in Balaj -- sorry, Brahimaj's custody in Jabllanice on about 25th July 1998, and next to Sali Berisha, the son of Misin Berisha and the evidence clearly establishes that his name featured, that is, Misin Berisha, as a collaborator on a KLA wanted list circulated in Baran by Haradinaj's appointed Din Krasniqi. Now, as you know both - and it's uncontested - died from gun-shot wounds in a similar matter to 18 other bodies found at the canal. Again, if you examine it in its totality and put those pieces into the picture, a pattern emerges showing that they must have been murdered pursuant to the joint criminal enterprise. Now, Mr. Emmerson made another somewhat curious submission yesterday when he said that there was no evidence in Counts 5 and 6 of ethnically motived violence, but he did it quite carefully by confining it to the treatment of Rosa Radosevic. What he neglected to draw your attention to is something I drew your attention to two days ago is what was said to her son, an ethnic Serb, while KLA soldiers were beating him. It's set out at page 973 of the transcript, and it bears repeating: "The KLA soldiers cursed our Serbian mothers. What do you want? Do you know who we are? They used abusive language with respect to our Serbian mothers, claiming that this was their land, what are you doing here?" Et cetera. Et cetera. Is that a serious submission that that violence wasn't ethnically motivated? Surely not, and surely not when put in the context of the coordinated KLA campaign to prevent ethnic Serbs returning to their homes in the area in Ramush Haradinaj's and Idriz Balaj's headquarters. Just going back a bit, three days before this brutal and completely ethnically motivated attack, Veselin Stijovic was held captive at Ramush Haradinaj's KLA headquarters in Gllogjan and brutally beaten. While he was there, the KLA commander of Ljumbarda, Deli Lekaj warned Stijovic who was from Dashinoc, that if he managed to escape Gllogjan alive he should never go back to Dashinoc because the KLA was planning to set up a roadblock in Pozar. At page 2138 of the transcript he said: "He told me, If they let you go alive, don't ever go back to Dasinovac because it's just a matter of time before we put up a roadblock on the road leading to Dasinovac in the village of Pozar." Now, that, Your Honours, is precisely what the KLA did. And when the KLA stopped -- KLA soldiers stopped Rosa Radosevic, Novak Stijovic, and Stanisa Radosevic at the Pozar roadblock, they searched the two cars and told them that the three had "no business anymore" in the area and could not go home. The KLA was preventing Serb civilians going home. Where did they take them? They took them to Gllogjan. What happened on the way? The ethnically motivated violence that Mr. Emmerson sidesteps. On the way KLA soldiers who saw arrested Serbs raise their fists and chanted, KLA, they were taken to Gllogjan and beaten. Now, as an aside I remind you of Witness 17's evidence, of his understanding of the meaning of being "taken to Gllogjan," it's been displayed now at page 7579 of the transcript where he said that: "Tahir Zemaj," that's the FARK commander, "said that if someone was detained and sent -- taken to Gllogjan and if his whereabouts are unknown, then it is Toger's responsibility," that's Balaj, "who carried out these detentions. And that's why the villagers were interested in these things and provided Tahir with information on these incidents, since something was wrong. It was said that the missing persons, those who that were detained and who went missing, these persons were sent to Gllogjan." Now, during the beating that followed Veselin Stijovic, the KLA soldiers insulted their ethnicity, interrogated them about their knowledge of and connections with the Serbian police, and told them to leave the area and go to Serbia. If that's not ethnically motivated violence, I don't know what is. Those three were lucky. They escaped. But the evidence proves beyond reasonable doubt that the KLA, members acting pursuant to the common criminal purpose, did not want those Serb civilians to return to their homes. They wanted to keep them out of the area. They wanted them to "return" to Serbia, although of course these people were long-standing residents of Kosovo. This evidence provides strong evidence of the persecutory intention of those within the common criminal purpose. Now, Witness 28, an unbiased, neutral, and in our submission impressive witness, a human rights monitor working under very difficult conditions gave evidence that in the last week of April 1998, that's in the time I've just referred to, she went to Decan and carefully counted that 34 Serb families had left villages in the Dukagjini area. She estimated by her careful counting that there had been some 123 Serb families living there in early 1998, although she said this figure may have involved -- included those living in the refugee settlement in Babaloc. Mr. Emmerson asked you to carefully consider the role of Ramush Haradinaj. We ask you to do the same. And when assessing his role in the KLA and his prominence in the Dukagjini Zone, you have to consider the nature of command and you have to consider it in the context. That's the context of the power vacuum created by the withdrawal of Serbian authority from the zone by mid-April 1998. Now, this was a vacuum that allowed a young, ambitious, strong, powerful, and charismatic personality like Ramush Haradinaj to step into and to consolidate his personal power over civilian and military matters in the coming months. And it's in that context that the horizontal structure that Mr. Emmerson suggested existed becomes a tool of the common criminal purpose to purge the zone of its enemies by unlawful means. You only have to look at who the main participants were. Family members of both Lahi Brahimaj and Ramush Haradinaj, Daut Haradinaj, Shkelzen Haradinaj, Nasim Haradinaj, Nazmi Brahimaj. In a sense Mr. Emmerson is quite correct. In April/May 1998 the KLA was no normal army. It was an army in its infancy and desperate for the experience of JNA officers like Rrustem Tetaj. It just did not have the classic two-up/two-down command structure of the JNA or the VJ. That's why the common criminal purpose worked. It worked because Haradinaj was a hands-on commander. He wasn't someone who commanded from behind; he was constantly at the front lines. But he's not charged with command responsibility. He's charged with participating in a common criminal purpose involving both his subordinates and others. And it was this lack of rigid formalised command structure, at least in the traditional military sense, that allowed the common criminal purpose to develop and flourish. And the evidence has proved that those outside of the common criminal purpose, professional military officers like Witness 17 and Tahir Zemaj, wanted no part in the structure that developed under Ramush Haradinaj's hand; rather, they wanted a proper military with the members subject to normal and proper military discipline. But this, Your Honours, is the last thing that Ramush Haradinaj wanted; and why, because proper military discipline entails educating soldiers in the laws of war, the conventions of war, and punishing those subordinates who breached them. And doing that, as the evidence has proved, will be the very antithesis of the common criminal purpose as we have proved. As we have set out in our final trial brief, it was this very lack of discipline, this culture of impunity, and the use of so-called military police as instruments of the common criminal purpose that allowed the members of this joint criminal enterprise to achieve their aim. Now, Mr. Emmerson quite correctly pointed out that Haradinaj's military police regulations don't advocate the mistreatment of prisoners of the KLA. Well, of course they don't. Haradinaj may be accused of war crimes, but he's not accused of stupidity, and certainly he wasn't stupid enough to put something like that in writing. What they do say, displaying on the screen, that's Exhibit P893, was, regulation 4, they had to investigate and uncover all those who collaborated with the enemy and were obliged to take measures against all those working against the KLA. And it was in the context of an undisciplined military police with no formal disciplinary system or court system that it allowed the military police, as an instrument of this joint criminal enterprise, to take whatever summary measures it wanted against "those working against the KLA," regulation 4, those suspected of collaboration. But what was in writing? What was most explicitly in writing was the names of those wanted. These names were on Haradinaj's appointee, Din Krasniqi's list. And in his trusted Lieutenant Balaj's pocketbook which he carried around with him. KLA training officer, Cufe Krasniqi, testified that every KLA soldier had the duty to report collaborators. And in the context of his evidence here, that can only refer to soldiers in Dukagjini under Haradinaj's command. The same lack of stupidity I referred to earlier, the same rationale applies when Haradinaj let the ECMM monitors, whom Balaj had detained and after beating up their Albanian interpreter, Haradinaj let them go. Haradinaj had to let them go and in a nice manner. He wasn't dumb. He knew that this was going to be reported back to the ECMM. Now, the reason that you won't find any Serb names on the wanted lists is because anyone with a Serb name was an automatic target of the KLA, members in the JCE, the joint criminal enterprise. An identity card would be enough for condemnation. If you look at the slide which will be shown on the screen now, it shows that all victims on the KLA wanted lists or otherwise wanted by the KLA did not have Serbian names. If you look at the names on the screen, they all have Albanian names. And if you look, it shows you where the victims ended up: Six by the canal, one buried at Jablanica, and one escaped. Another two pieces of evidence are those of -- that when Witness 6 and Nenad Remistar were abducted at the same time, Witness 6, a Kosovar Catholic civilian was accused of spying for Serbia, imprisoned, beaten, and then released. Remistar, however, an ethnic Serb traffic police officer, was murdered just after 24 hours. And contrary to Mr. Emmerson's description of Haradinaj's allegedly cordial relationship with the opposition supporting FARK is the evidence of Witness 17 who met Haradinaj on the 10th of July, 1998, and this is after the incident when the supposedly calm and rational commander pistol-whipped a FARK soldier six days earlier. Witness 17 in Exhibit P885 at paragraphs 42 to 43 describes Haradinaj's behaviour on that day as acting like "someone unstable, on drugs. His actions were inconsistent." Returning to Mr. Emmerson's submission in relation to the ethnic cleansing or the attacks on Serbian houses in the Dukagjini area, they were not random; they were systematic. And put it in its geographical context and for what these types of comparisons are worth, it's not a large zone. Compared to, say, The Hague it's about three times the size of The Hague's municipal boundaries. And Mr. Emmerson tried to deflect attention away from the KLA stated policy of attacking the Serb colonizer or occupier as they were called by suggesting that the Serb civilians left the Dukagjini area because of ethnic tensions caused by the minority status within the repressive Serbian, that is, Milosevic, regime. But the evidence establishes a well-organized and synchronised attack on Serb settlements in a single night, the first day of the indictment period, the 1st to 2nd of March, 1998, and I take you to Zoran Stijovic's evidence where he testified that eight synchronised attacks in six different villages in Klina and Gjakove municipalities on that night, and that's paragraph 37 of P931. Now, breaking those down, you can see on the screen what he's referring to. The official notes, that's P967 and 968 demonstrate they were clearly synchronised. On the 1st of March at 10.15 p.m. there was an attack on a MUP housing facility in Erec. On the 2nd of March early in the morning at 1.00 a.m. there was an attack on family houses in Bec in Djakovica. At 1.00 a.m. there was an attack on the house of Belic in Stepanica in Klina. At 2.00 a.m. there was an attack on the Fatic house in Crmljane. At 2.00 a.m. there was an attack in Dolovo on a Serb house, Garic. At 3.00 a.m. there was an attack on the Nedavic [phoen] house in Karpus [phoen] in Klina. Now, I won't repeat my submissions in relation to the strength of recognition evidence about Ramush Haradinaj and his neighbours who grew up next to him and went to school with him. But I ask you to consider this: Had the events involving the Stojanovics in Counts 3 and 4 happened in the manner suggested by Mr. Emmerson, a sort of spontaneous uprising of villagers against the Stijovics -- the Stojanovics and Stijovics, where was Haradinaj when this was occurring? Why would he not have been there attempting to control this mob and impose discipline on his soldiers and the civilians who were severely mistreating these Serbs? In the context of all the evidence you have heard about his presence and management style, he had to have been there, and that's supported by the direct evidence that he was there. Where did the KLA soldiers take these people? Straight to KLA headquarters in Gllogjan. Whose headquarters? Ramush Haradinaj's. The evidence is entirely consistent with Haradinaj's role within the joint criminal enterprise. Other KLA soldiers including his brother Daut commenced the attack and Ramush Haradinaj later arrived on the scene at his own headquarters joined in the attack by kicking a man lying hard on the ground who was already suffering serious internal injuries. Now, going briefly to Mr. Emmerson's submission about the strength of Mijat Stojanovic's recognition evidence, what Mr. Emmerson didn't submit of course was the completely plausible explanation for why Mijat didn't mention Ramush Haradinaj's name at the time. And the Prosecution of course we readily concede that in the context of this particularly brutal assault, and the Defence does not deny there was a brutal assault, Ramush Haradinaj's role was more minor but only insofar as it was the others who were beating the victims with rifle-butts. But Mijat Stojanovic explained this to you at trial when Mr. Emmerson showed the Article D25, and it's on the screen now, he asked, Why didn't you mention his name on the day? His answer was: "Nobody asked me at the time ... I'm not talking about the names I saw; I'm talking about the names that beat me." And in relation to the presence of Daut Haradinaj he said that when was asked him -- was told that there was no mention: "Well, that may be the case. I have no idea what the journalists wrote. I am certain that Daut was among them. Journalists include or omit whatever they like. It's not my place to judge that." This is not a case of delayed memory or recognition and Mr. Emmerson's reliance on the Kupreskic appeal judgement at paragraph 40 is misplaced. The case is entirely indistinguishable because if you go back to the Canadian Supreme Court case it relies on, it had nothing to do with ID evidence. It related to a trial where the Judge found that one witness was so unreliable his evidence required corroboration. The facts here could not be more different. Mijat Stojanovic and Dragoslav Stojanovic knew Ramush Haradinaj. The body recovery operation. It was imperfect, we concede that, we recognise it. It was in a war zone. It was an area retaken only after a massive Serbian offensive referred to in Zivanovic's and Crosland's evidence. Judge Gojkovic just did not have the resources to undertake the massive exercise of examining a crime scene containing a mass grave and spread over a distance of a kilometre using local MUP officials. He had to summons help from Belgrade and assemble a forensic team, and that took time. Two days, in fact. They had to drive many hours from Belgrade. It was an area vulnerable to attack. It was deep within enemy territory. It had been held, as Witness 17 said, by the KLA in his time since he'd been there. The facilities were so basic they had to set up a morgue in the basement of a hotel. The team was working under what Professor Aleksandric described as war conditions. They stopped when a missile exploded. And if you look at paragraph 243 of Aleksandric's statement on the screen, Exhibit P1260, he explains it. "A shell flew over the canyon and fell on to the other side." And at page 6814 of the transcript, asked to say where it came from and who fired, he said: "Somebody fired a mortar at us. We were told it was a mortar by an experienced policemen who had been in combat there for months." That was enough to send them flying. Judge Gojkovic ordered work to cease. But if we just go back to the crime scene for a moment to show how it was uncovered. When the large photograph comes up on the screen, you can see from the overview where the bodies were located. They were next to the canal and they were up to 1 kilometre downstream from it. That's a lot of bodies over a big area. Now, Mr. Emmerson's submission about KLA captives Kalamashi, Alija, and Musaj taking the -- the suspicion you should view what happened there is, to use an English expression, a classic red herring. We concede readily that they may have been mistreated in custody and the custodial records are severely lacking. But the evidence is only of an investigatory lead. We wouldn't suggest for one moment you could use the evidence against them in a case or as a confession. The important thing is they took the Serbs to the canal. And what did the Serbs find when they got there? Judge Gojkovic described it in his statement, that's P1193, paragraph 24, where it says: "We came to the canal. I saw bullet-holes in the canal wall and bodies at the wall of the canal." At paragraph 29 -- 28: "I saw bodies dressed in civilian clothes. I saw body parts at the wall. My impression of the scene was of a very gruesome sight with bodies and body parts all over the place, the smell, the flies, the blood, it was a terrible sight. I observed bodies covered by the soil and by the wall at the canal. I crossed the canal and saw more bodies and body parts." Now, it's worth revisiting in response to Mr. Emmerson's submissions about the body recovery, the bullet-holes, and you can see them there on the screen at P416. The bullet-holes were clearly on the inside and outside of the canal wall near the bodies. Colonel Crosland, a very experienced military officer, independent, neutral, an impressive witness in our submission, described them as splash marks caused in his view by bursts of automatic fire and some single shots from a distance of about 10 to 20 metres. This is not consistent with, as Mr. Emmerson would like you to believe, an exchange of fire across a -- across the canal. And the Frrokaj's canal -- sorry, car was lying in the canal just below the water, and it's worth -- it's worth pausing here just for a moment to recap their evidence of what happened the Frrokajs who were last seen entering Gllogjan through the KLA check-point. The only way out past that check-point was either back through the check-point they went in through or at the KLA check-point on the other side or there's a third alternative, taking the road to the canal. Well, where did the car end up? You can see on Exhibit P64 exactly where it ended up with Illira Frrokaj's body in the trunk or boot and both containing signs of burning. Another red herring is what Witness 21 saw or didn't see when he went there. There's a very obvious explanation for what he saw. He could not have seen that car there or the bodies as they were strewn along that one kilometre covered by vegetation in part from where he was standing. The evidence is also clear that those who went to the canal looking for the Frrokajs' bodies feared meeting Toger, Balaj, and even devised a plan of self-defence in the event of meeting him. We submit that Shkelzen's offer of assistance like his brother Ramush's to the family of Sanije Balaj was nothing more, in the circumstances, a public relations sham. Now, Achilleas Pappas, another neutral person, also went to the canal and what did he see when he got there? P271, which will be on the screen in a moment, describes him seeing bullet marks, which obviously in his opinion killed these people. He said it was common sense. At paragraph 23, based on his experience he said there was no doubt that the mass grave was directly linked to the KLA presence in this area. My opinion is based upon the following. It was located in an area controlled by the KLA until they had to retreat due to a Serb attack at the end of August/beginning of September, and based on the level of putrefaction it was clear they were killed some time before they were found. There was no single Serb presence in this area until that attack. Now, the existence of this mass grave was also an open secret amongst the KLA in the Dukagjini area but not everybody could stomach it, Your Honours. On the 20th of August, 1998, Mr. Emmerson made some submissions about this, just three weeks before the Serbian forces discovered this mass grave, the topic of KLA crimes and the bodies in the canal was raised at a meeting of 68 KLA village commanders in Prapaqan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Re, a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Haradinaj -- I'm sorry. Are we there? Haradinaj sat at the front -- at a table at the front of the room and Rrok Berisha, a FARK member, stood up in a voice loud enough for everyone to hear asked for the KLA to stop committing crimes, declaring the fish in Lake Radoniq were getting fat on human flesh. Now, this is corroborated by another source, it came from Witness 17 because it was also known to the DB which had three or four sources at that particular meeting, which is page 9090 of Mr. Stijovic's testimony. Mr. Guy-Smith seemingly attacked the Prosecution on its choice of witnesses, but like parties to litigation anywhere in the world you can't choose your witnesses; you take them as they come. In the accusings of cherry-picking, I remind the Trial Chamber that we applied for 21 subpoenas, of which you issued 18, which is unprecedented in the Tribunal's history as a total percentage of testifying witnesses. And our proposed witness order was thrown out the window within weeks because witnesses refusing to testify against the accused. As you know, eventually only four refused to testify, two in Kosovo, one in the United States and Canada, but of these four, the Trial Chamber, not the Prosecution, indicted -- the Prosecution's indictment of two of them, three for contempt. And Avni Krasniqi and Sadri Selca given numerous warnings and offers of transportation to The Hague had to be indicted and brought here to testify. In assessing the evidence against his client, you have to consider some consider -- some compelling similarities, and in particular, Balaj's modus operandi because Mr. Guy-Smith's submissions were devoted to recognition of identification. The victims about who you have heard direct evidence of his personal attacks have a number of similarities. I will deal with eight. First, they were all women. One he raped after taking to her -- to his headquarters; the other three, all members of the Serb collaborating family, he abducted. The three were then murdered. Second, he visited their homes late at night. Third, he came to these women's homes with armed soldiers. Fourth, he commanded these armed soldiers. Fifth, the soldiers called him Toger. Sixth, he took Sister S and the rape victim to the KLA headquarters in Irzniq. Seventh, Toger wore black clothes, just like the Toger you can see in the Baran swearing-in video. Eighth, the victims in both counts, families, the rape victim -- not the -- families clearly identified a clearly recognised Balaj from photo identification boards as the Toger in question. Now, of course Sanije Balaj, whose bullet-ridden body was dumped at the canal, was also a woman. Another similarity is that his counsel, Mr. Guy-Smith, did not suggest to Witness 4, Witness 19, or to the rape victim -- did not suggest to the rape victim that no one called Toger came to their houses, abducted family members, or in the case of the rape victim, raped her. He did not suggest or put a case that the soldiers who came with Toger -- the soldier did not identify himself as Toger. He didn't put to Witness 4 that Toger did not introduce himself to the witness as Toger. The reason is obvious. There was only one Toger, an outsider, as Mr. Guy-Smith rightly concedes, and one whose name, Idriz Balaj, was not generally known then. But they all knew who Toger was even if they didn't know his name. And by process of elimination, there being no other Toger in the zone, much less one matching the description of Idriz Balaj, the only conclusion available on the evidence is that Toger, the Toger who personally committed the crimes charged, is Idriz Balaj. Exhibit 1230 shows photo identification made by another witness of the rapist Toger as Balaj, that's number 6. Witness 17, who knew Balaj in 1998 identified Toger as Balaj without photo-boards. Avni Krasniqi identified Toger by name as Idriz Balaj. Now, the reasons Mr. Guy-Smith suggests for Avni Krasniqi to manufacture a story about Balaj's involvement in the disposal of Sanije Balaj's body are so far-fetched and fanciful as not even to bear cursory examination before you summarily reject them. He made a ludicrous and unsupported assertion that Avni Krasniqi received benefits including, and I don't know what including means, they're not informing, that's us, the cooperating state of Switzerland, a person they knew was wanted was in custody and they let him go in exchange for his testimony. All aspects of that assertion are false. Avni Krasniqi was one of the most reluctant witnesses ever to come before this Tribunal. Not only did he refuse to obey a subpoena and ignore an order given to the Prosecution to indict -- to investigate him for contempt, a Kosovo investigator gave him an attempt to have him testify voluntarily. The Trial Chamber, not the OTP, indicted Krasniqi for contempt, and he was given another opportunity after his arrest but before his transfer to come voluntarily rather than as an indictee. And he was never in the Prosecution's custody; he was in the Tribunal's custody. And the Prosecution had no contact with him between his arrival here and his departure, apart from in court. It's on public record, page 10772, and all contact was through his lawyer, Mr. Pestman who was not aware of the sentences in Switzerland committed some 13 years ago -- sorry, imposed some 13 years ago in absentia. He did not even know until after he had informed the deputy registrar and then the Prosecution that his client was going to testify. It was not an inducement, had nothing to do with it. And when Mr. Krasniqi testified, his evidence was entirely consistent of that he gave in the trial of Galani in Kosovo. He's never wavered in saying that Idriz Balaj took or ordered the body to be exhumed and took it away. No plausible or credible reason exists for him to falsely accuse Balaj of this. He was the only witness. If he was going to accuse Balaj of something, why not the murder? The truth is he told the truth. He got absolutely nothing out of testifying and he did not want to be here, and Idriz Balaj as an outsider had absolutely zero connection with any supposed blood-feud between the Krasniqi family and Sanije Balaj's family in the Baran valley area. Avni Krasniqi didn't know where Balaj took the body. He only says he saw him driving off with it. And crucially, which shows what a house of cards this is, the DNA identification of Sanije Balaj's body was not confirmed until the 28th of May last year, almost two weeks after Avni Krasniqi testified in Kosovo on the 16th of May. He could not have known that R-1 was Sanije Balaj's body, nor that it was on top of Witness 4's mother and sister. The only person who probably knew that was Idriz Balaj. I want to take you to a submission in relation to Ylber Haskaj's evidence and I just want to demonstrate with a map or a photograph, and that's the photograph at Exhibit 1217 which was where he said the Black Eagles were. Now, if you put on top of that, and we've got a Google Earth photograph showing where that actually was, you can see it was within that square zone and that is entirely between where Ramush Haradinaj's house is which is to the right of the photograph and the Ekonomija farm which is to the left. So although we say he wasn't particularly reliable on this point, where he says the Black Eagles was is also in that area right between the Haradinaj family compound, the Ekonomija farm, and the canal. We have some -- we can provide copies of that in hard copy if the Trial Chamber wants them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Turning to Lahi Brahimaj, now Mr. Harvey complained yesterday I hadn't devoted enough attention to developing the case against his client. I'm happy to oblige him by turning to some points, and we of course emphasise that Lahi Brahimaj is no Nelson Mandela and this Tribunal isn't the Pretoria Supreme Court in South Africa in 1964 at the height of apartheid. And if you look at the evidence as he invited me to do so, and this is the evidence that convicts his client, I make these points: Brahimaj participated in savagely beating prisoners at Jabllanice barracks. He participated in beating Witness 6. He tricked Witness 3 into going there. Witness 3 was immediately beaten with baseball bats by other KLA soldiers. He was often present there and in the same room where Witness 6 was imprisoned between 13th of June and 25th of July. He must have seen or must have been aware of the shocking mistreatment and torture meted out to Pal Krasniqi, a Bosnian, three Montenegrins, and Skender Kuci. He took Witness 3 from his room into an adjoining room where Witness 3 was beaten by women KLA soldiers, encouraged to commit suicide, and threatened with execution. Brahimaj himself accused him of spying, but fortunately Witness 3 could escape. Brahimaj abducted Witness 3 at gunpoint a second time, beat him, and threatened him. He showed great concern to the now-deceased Skender Kuci, having offered 10.000 marks to Witness 3 to help him escape. Brahimaj took Witness 3 to Gllogjan to imprison him there, although the commander later released him. Brahimaj moved prisoners, took prisoners to Jablanica, and tortured them. The evidence is clear, it's in Witness 6, Witness 3, and is also very strong identification evidence which wasn't really challenged. In relation to Mr. Harvey's legal point, clearly the word "next to" should be read to mean "near to." Nothing turns on that at all. It's not a material particular or a charge, it's a slight misstatement of geographic position of two KLA buildings in Jablanica. His other point can also likewise be dismissed by putting it into perspective. It's the fact that Brahimaj condoned and encouraged criminal capacity -- criminal conduct in his capacity as a commander, that is important. And even on just the wording of the indictment, that would be a relevant factor to consider in assessing the importance of his contribution. The pre-trial brief simply corrects a minor clarification of an existing allegation in the indictment. The accused has been on notice since before the trial of the case, he has had a fair trial, there is no investigation needed, he needed no time to investigate, he was there, he knows exactly what happened. One point I do emphasise, though, is that Brahimaj was a proud member of the General Staff, sometimes also called the central staff. But this is the same General Staff that was proudly proclaimed responsibility for murdering Serb civilians and collaborators in the years, months, and days directly before the conflict in 1998. His lawyers don't deny the accuracy of the minutes of the meeting of the 23rd of June, 1998, in which it is recorded that he had been a member of the secret central staff since 1993. And the General Staff spokesperson, Jakup Krasniqi, even admitted in Exhibit P328 about the -- about the suffering of the KLA collaborators where he said: Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serb civilians. You've seen the communiques which showed the KLA had long-standing and openly stated policy of liquidating collaborators. The evidence of this is incontrovertible. I refer you also to Jakup Krasniqi's testimony in Limaj which is Exhibit P340 here and the fact that Zoran Stijovic testified to the accuracy of these communiques which the Defence attempts to dismiss as mere propaganda; they weren't. The context is that if you look at the communiques up till 29th of April, 1998, which is annex 12 of the Krasniqi statement, P328, it was then when the international community was present that the KLA, so to speak, decided to launch itself with a new image internationally, and that was just after the United Nations Security Council had passed Resolution 1160 on the 31st of March: "Condemning all acts of terrorism by the KLA." It was only at that point that the KLA issued that communique, saying that it condemns terrorism and other violations of the civilian population. But as the evidence has proved, so far as the KLA and those participating in the joint criminal enterprise was concerned, it was business as usual in their attacks on civilians and alleged collaborators.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The similarities in this case, as I opened with two days ago, are so compelling that the only conclusion is of the guilt of the accused. The bodies were all disposed of in an area less than 2 kilometres from Haradinaj's house, in an area controlled by the KLA, within the control of the Gllogjan staff, which was Ramush Haradinaj's power base throughout the indictment period. He was by far the dominant military leader based on his personal -- direct personal relations with KLA village leaders. He concerned himself with every aspect of military and civilian affairs. As a formal matter, he was head of the Gllogjan staff. He directly engaged in acts of violence against his Serb neighbours. He issued orders for the detention of suspected collaborators and several of those who disappeared were, indeed, arrested on that basis by members of the KLA. The evidence, in our submission, is damning, it's overwhelming. The only conclusion you can reach on the totality of the evidence is that Haradinaj, Balaj, and Brahimaj are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of all of the crimes charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you'll be the first one to --

utterances.text: Yes, thank you, and we've discussed allocation of time between ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
