utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What I want to do in my rebuttal and rejoinder is to look at eight pillars of the Prosecution case, as Mr. Re has sought to draw them out in his submissions yesterday and today, in order to illustrate what we suggested to the Trial Chamber at the outset of our submissions; namely, that once the component elements of the Prosecution case are subjected to searching judicial scrutiny, the glib superficial and broad-brush inferences that the Prosecution invites you to draw are ultimately shown to be based upon a contrived interpretation of both documentary and testimonial evidence. Let me start with persecutory intent. Yesterday and at two points in their closing brief the Prosecution drew the Trial Chamber's attention to a set of minutes of the Gllogjan staff dated the 9th of July which they assert included a threat from the Dobrigje representatives to attack two Montenegrin households in the village and which they say was then borne out a few days later when those houses were in fact attacked. The Albanian original of the exhibit to which Mr. Re referred at transcript 11062 yesterday is P190. As it happens, there is no official translation uploaded into e-court, which is presumably why it wasn't put up on the screen by Mr. Re. The Prosecution has, in fact, based its reading of those minutes on a draft translation which is inaccurate and has not been agreed. The Defence translation of this document reads that there are ten individuals able to go and get weapons, but even on the draft translation used by the Prosecution - and bear in mind, there is no translation to which they have drawn your attention of the minutes as a whole - but even on the draft translation that the Prosecution is working from, the minutes don't contain any threat at all. It's taken completely and utterly out of context. What the minutes show is each village in turn reporting back on the situation as it is in the ground, who lives in the village, the size of the population, the number of men available to fight, their weapons, their state of readiness in case of Serb attack, and the entry for the Dobrigje representative makes no threat at all. It simply lists the number of households and the number of people ready to fight. However, there's no reliably sourced evidence concerning the alleged attack by the KLA on the households in Dobrigje. The 92 ter statement of Witness 68 on which they rely says in terms that she knows nothing about the details of the attack or who perpetrated it, and she was asked no questions about it during her testimony. It is, regrettably, a case in which the Trial Chamber is going to need to subject every single, every single, assertion that the Prosecution makes to a level of scrutiny that Judges shouldn't really have to apply when examining submissions made by those representing prosecuting authorities because they ought to be able to trust the accuracy and the fairness of the way in which matters are put. But this is a case that has been put together throughout by selectivity, decontextualization and contrived interpretation. Let me give you another example from really the second major pillar of the Prosecution case. Mr. Re suggests to you that the military police were an integral part of the joint criminal enterprise and were used by Ramush Haradinaj to hunt down suspected opponents and to kill them. But the entire basis upon which that -- those allegations, that assessment, is put forward is based upon - to put it generously - insufficiently close attention to the detail of what the evidence actually shows. There is no evidence at all in this case of any crime, even allegedly, being committed by any member of the military police appointed by Ramush Haradinaj. The only evidence of their activities relates to the investigations conducted by Fadil Nimonaj into the investigation of the death of Sanije Balaj and of the disappearance of Nurije and Istref Krasniqi. The story is very clearly told in four exhibits and I'll just for the record give the references, P140, P893, D60, and P224, a series of records which show how, when, and why the military police that Ramush Haradinaj set up came to be established. A number of points emerge. First of all, there is no evidence at all, indeed there is evidence to the contrary, that the regional staff created on the 26th of May ever had a military police. The first reference to a military police unit in any minutes of any meeting within Mr. Haradinaj's area of responsibility arises on the 21st of June, the meeting at which the military police regulations were adopted. That is P140. The Trial Chamber reads those minutes. It is as clear as it possibly can be that what takes place at that meeting is a preliminary discussion on the proposal with different drafts of police regulations circulated and a discussion on what the function and role of a military police should be. Rrustem Tetaj who was at that meeting told you - and the Prosecution didn't seek to undermine this evidence - that no military police unit was in fact set up at that meeting on the 21st of June. D60 are the minutes of a meeting on the 25th of July of the newly formed operational staff. Those minutes take the next stage in the story forward. They record the steps which had been taken in the interim towards the formation of this unit and the appointment of Tigri, Fadil Nimonaj as its commander. They note that the FARK brigades, which of course by then had been established, "support the idea of a military police." It's clear from the minutes themselves that a military police unit was not formed by the Dukagjini Plain Operational Zone any earlier than the 25th of July, something that was confirmed directly in testimony by Rrustem Tetaj and by Shemsedin Cekaj, both of whom attended the meeting, and the footnote references are in our brief. And the matter is put beyond doubt at P224, a report by Mr. Haradinaj to the General Staff of the 28th of July saying we have now formed a military police. So we have the clearest possible evidence as to how, when, and where the military police unit was formed. What the evidence does show, though, is that other autonomous military police groupings were set up in two of the areas that fell outside Mr. Haradinaj's area of responsibility prior to the establishment of the Dukagjini operational zone on the 23rd of June, Pjeter Shala and his documentation for the formation of a military police, which states clearly that the military police that he described himself as being a member of, a so-called unit, reports to the commander of the local staff from which it receives its orders, and the two self-styled policemen wandering around the Baran valley, Mete and Avni Krasniqi, who, it will be recalled, came from Vranoc, an area right on the edge of the territory covered by the regional staff established on the 26th of May, but right on the edge of the zone that was commanded as subzone-commander by Rrustem Tetaj. So if they had been appointed in any sense through the framework of the regional staff, then they would have been appointed by Rrustem Tetaj. But his testimony, as the Prosecution acknowledges and reminds you, is that this man was not someone that he appointed; indeed, that Mete Krasniqi, he thought, had been appointed on his own personal initiative. In other words, he walked around proclaiming himself to be a member of the military police. But that doesn't suit the Prosecution's case. It requires too much penetration of the detail and disentitles them to make a broad-brush allegation that crimes on this indictment were committed by Mr. Haradinaj's military police. It's just not true. Let me go to the third pillar, lists, target lists says Mr. Re. Target lists circulated by Din Krasniqi, who had been appointed by Ramush Haradinaj. What he's referring to of course is Exhibit P885, the private notes written by Witness 17 in his own notebook following a meeting on the 12th of July at which he appointed a military police unit. Those notes for the record are dealt with in our brief at paragraphs 149 to 150, 484 to 488, 509 to 511, and 597 to 598. When he was cross-examined about this list - and the Trial Chamber described his testimony at the time in the course of cross-examination as evasive - when he was cross-examined about this list Witness 17 said first of all that he didn't know who had given him the names, nor did he know why the people were being sought or who was looking for them. But the critical thing is that the Prosecution's attempt to try to ramrod this into Mr. Haradinaj's responsibility is based on nothing. There is nothing to connect that list to Mr. Haradinaj, and as I emphasised yesterday at transcript 7700, I asked Witness 17: "Did you ever tell Mr. Haradinaj about this list?" And he said: "No." One of the names on the list was Skender Kuci's name. Well, we know - and it's not challenged by the Prosecution - that when Ramush Haradinaj was told about the detention of Skender Kuci, he intervened. So to suggest that this was a list of people who were being hunted on his behalf is completely contradictory to the evidence, but that doesn't suit the Prosecution because they don't want the Trial Chamber to dig deep or to penetrate. It's worth, again, just contemplating what that intervention in practical terms involved. It occurred, as the Trial Chamber is aware, at the or during the second half of July, just as the Serb forces were beginning the first serious stages of the summer offensive. On the 13th of July you will remember Colonel Crosland had reported increasing evidence of wanton damage to the villages in Decan, and by the 28th of July, two weeks later, he was reporting that every village from Lapushnik westwards had been attacked with cannon and heavy mortar. And it was in that context that Mr. Haradinaj left the front line and made the journey to Jabllanice in order to direct the release of a man he knew little or nothing about. And on the evidence that you've heard when he did so, he gave an injunction that nothing of the kind should ever happen again. So the inclusion of Skender Kuci's name on the list hardly supports the Prosecution case theory. Witness 17, when asked by Mr. Kearney whether Mr. Haradinaj had raised the issue of collaborators in the 20 or so meetings they had together, said that he never once raised the topic. Transcript 7565. The Prosecution sought to argue that Mr. Haradinaj or the Gllogjan headquarters had a list of its own and there is a completely factually inaccurate allegation in a 92 ter statement of Zoran Stijovic, the man upon whom the Prosecution invites you to draw inferences about the activity of the KLA, where it is alleged at paragraph 42 that the MUP found a target list of Serb spies at the Gllogjan headquarters of Mr. Haradinaj after the 24th of March operation. In fact, the report that Mr. Stijovic purported to produce made no such -- gave no such foundation. It stated in terms that the MUP had found address books with names in them and they didn't know one way or the other whether these were lists of KLA members, KLA supporters, or possible targets, and the Trial Chamber then declined to admit the document. There's no evidence at all of a hit list or a target list from Gllogjan. What then do the Prosecution say about Witness 17's list? First of all, they say Zenun Gashi's name was on the list, and so it was. Well, if the dates that were supplied by Witness 52 are correct and Zenun Gashi was taken from his home on the 1st of August by Vesel Dizdari on the orders of Mete Krasniqi, Witness 17 was given that list about two and a half weeks before Zenun Gashi was arrested. And so the most obvious inference the Trial Chamber may think is that the group of military police that he chose and appointed - and he said in terms, they were given to me as a list of proposals and I accepted them and I presided over the election of their commander Hasan Gashi - had it in mind that Zenun Gashi was somebody in whom they were interested. That list, that is to say of military police officers, included Iber Krasniqi as an approved member of Witness 17's police force, the cousin of Mete Krasniqi, on whose orders Zenun Gashi was taken. There's no evidence at all that Zenun Gashi was taken to Gllogjan. He was taken and deposited at the FARK barracks that is the clear evidence of Vesel Dizdari and it is corroborated by the evidence of Sadri Selca. Misin Berisha's name is on the list. Well, if Witness 17 was telling you the truth and this was a list of both missing and wanted persons - in other words, it wasn't a list as he told you of people who were necessarily there because they were thought to be collaborators - then you need, as with Zenun Gashi, to look at the time-frame. The evidence of Luan Tetaj establishes no clear date for the disappearance of Misin Berisha and his sons. He was only able to say that they went missing sometime in June or July. In this instance, therefore, it's entirely possible that Misin Berisha was already known to be missing at the time that Witness 17 had the meeting on the 12th of July. He may well be one of those whose name appeared on the list, not because he was being sought as a collaborator, but because someone at the meeting already knew that he was missing. But none of that, of course, suits the Prosecution's case because it would require the Trial Chamber to conduct too penetrating an analysis of the inferences that can properly be drawn. What about Nurije and Istref Krasniqi? What about the suggestion yesterday that their names were on that list? The entry on that list and the only one that could possibly refer to Nurije and Istref Krasniqi reads as follows: "The conflict in Turjake, one person wounded, entrance wound on a side of the neck and exit on the other side, with the destruction of the central neural system." Witness 17 said that that was a reference to a conflict between two families who lived in Turjake village. Well, we know exactly who those two families were and who the person who was shot in the neck was. This was a reference to the shooting bound up in the blood-feud. The same note also contains an entry which records two women collaborators, Turjake Kosuriq, now of course that doesn't fit either because it's a reference to two women in two different villages, but says the Prosecution, you can twist it. You can infer that must be a reference to Nurije Krasniqi. Well, on what basis does the Prosecution say that? And anyway, what's it got to do with Ramush Haradinaj? It's not in his notebook. The lists, really, in order to buy the theory of the lists or to try to find any connection between Mr. -- I'm sorry, Witness 17's notebook and Ramush Haradinaj, the Prosecution are then driven to use the language of parallel structure to suggest that going on in the Baran valley under the command of Witness 17 was some independent structure. It's worth just pausing for a moment to recall what that suggestion is really based on, and we deal with it in our brief at paragraphs 80 to 91, 489 to 500, and 662 to 663. It's a point that the Prosecution cling on to in closing. Well, it was based on the proposition, first of all, that Witness 17 thought that Ramush Haradinaj had appointed Din Krasniqi in the first place. Again, a suggestion that Mr. Re made several times this afternoon. It was based secondly on Witness 17's understanding that Din Krasniqi continued to take directions and orders from Mr. Haradinaj and to have regular meetings with him after the opening of the FARK barracks, and it was based on his assertion in his 92 ter statement that Din Krasniqi also had contact during this period with Faton Mehmetaj and Idriz Balaj. The claim that Din Krasniqi was appointed or selected by Ramush Haradinaj is contradicted by the evidence of Zymer Hasanaj, Shaban Balaj, and Cufe Krasniqi, each of whom gave evidence that Din Krasniqi was elected by local villagers. Indeed, Cufe Krasniqi testified that he personally proposed Din Krasniqi as commander. When pressed in cross-examination as to the basis for his assertion, Witness 17 accepted that he had no personal knowledge of the manner in which Din Krasniqi came to be appointed, 7657, and that he had described him in an earlier witness statement as a self-proclaimed commander of Baran. Why? Because, as he explained in cross-examination, although Din Krasniqi claimed the authority of Ramush Haradinaj, Witness 17 had no official confirmation of this, 7752. What about continuing contacts? He was repeatedly pressed during cross-examination to provide a factual basis for his assertion that Din Krasniqi continued to report to Ramush Haradinaj after the brigade was established, and his answers, which the Trial Chamber will find at 7658 to 7664, were as evasive on that as they were on so many other matters. He accepted that he was never present at such a meeting, that he had no idea what if anything may have been discussed. Eventually, after much prevarication he suggested that certain village commanders had told him that Din Krasniqi was reporting to Ramush Haradinaj. So he was asked which commanders? And he said, I don't have a name. I don't know exactly the name. So the Trial Chamber asked him could he remember which village these commanders came from? No, he said, I don't have knowledge about the names. So he was asked whether the information had come from one or more than one village commander. And he said, I can't recall. So he was asked to describe the exact nature of the contact, and he said, I can't talk in details. At the time the Trial Chamber observed that to say that that evidence was very much supportive of ongoing contacts would be an overstatement, 7799. We respectfully agree. The only evidence of any contact between Ramush Haradinaj and Din Krasniqi after the formation of the brigades is a set of minutes P892 of a single meeting of Baran valley staffs on the 29th of July, just as the Serb offensives were about to hit Jabllanice, for example, which records Mr. Haradinaj's presence. In the context of the fragmented and confused command relationships which were then plainly in existence, that meeting can hardly be taken as evidence of a parallel command structure and there's nothing sinister about the meeting or secretive about it at all. Mr. Haradinaj remained as Dukagjin Operational Zone commander during this period, even though Witness 17 didn't seem to know, and neither did any of the other witnesses, who if anyone was really in command of who. In his Rule 92 ter statement, Witness 17 also claimed, as I said earlier, that Din Krasniqi had direct contacts during this period with Faton Mehmetaj and Idriz Balaj. Where that suggestion came from, nobody knows, because when he was asked about it during his testimony he accepted that he had no factual basis for it at all, 7799 and 7801 and 7802, but of course that would require a penetrating analysis of the theorizing of the Prosecution, and that's not something which they would invite the Trial Chamber to conduct. I touched yesterday - and I'm not going to go through it again - on the role of Mete Krasniqi and the very obviously close relationship he had with the FARK brigade at Baran, it's set out in detail of our brief at paragraphs 489 to 500. The evidence at its highest suggests that the former KLA volunteers from the Baran valley were disorganized and lacking in any effective command structure and that Witness 17 was unsuccessful in imposing discipline within his area of responsibility after the establishment of the FARK barracks. He said there was a kind of anarchy under the command that he encountered which posed an obstacle to the creation of a unified military command, 7664 to 7665. He said that when he got there he encountered disorganized groups which lacked structure and discipline. They had little or no respect for the chain of command. They were not well organized military units in the vertical sense, 7665. Well, no one disputes that the absence of organizational command which Witness 17 encountered on his arrival would have required a degree of coordination to ensure that the barracks operated effectively, but that was his job. None of this begins to establish the existence of a parallel command structure reporting to Ramush Haradinaj. All it shows is a failure on the part of Witness 17 to impose effective disciplinary steps within his area of responsibility, but there is no evidence that Ramush Haradinaj played any role at all in promoting the continued existence of a separate command. It was, after all, Witness 17 and not Ramush Haradinaj who tolerated the existence of a group of self-appointed policemen operating within metres of his command headquarters. The parallel structure theory, just like the lists theory, on penetrating analysis is a myth. Sanije Balaj, another limb or plank of the Prosecution's closing argument, and the suggestion as it was put to you was that there is independent corroboration for the evidence of Avni Krasniqi. He, says Mr. Re, this afternoon, is somebody who couldn't have been lying because he had no motive to lie. I don't know whether Mr. Re read the Prosecution's closing brief before making that argument, but they themselves assert in terms that Avni Krasniqi is lying because he obviously was about his involvement in the Sanije Balaj case because his evidence is flatly inconsistent with the evidence of Witness 72, of Cufe Krasniqi, of Shaban Balaj, of Witness 17, of every other witness in relation to that incident. He came here and said on oath to the Tribunal that he had nothing to do with stopping her or interrogating her. Once it's clear and once the Prosecution accepts that that evidence is not the truth, how they can then invite the Trial Chamber to proceed with confidence on uncorroborated allegations that he makes is very difficult to understand, but of course all that would require a level of penetration the Prosecution eschews. So yesterday it was suggested that there's corroboration for the allegation that Idriz Balaj moved the body. Where does the corroboration come from? It comes, says the Prosecution, from an official report compiled by Sadri Selca. That's P897 and we deal with it in our brief at paragraphs 721 to 725. It's quite right that Sadri Selca produced a so-called official report, although the reliability of anything said or recorded by Sadri Selca must be open to very serious doubt. But he testified that the basis for his information came from having to spoken to two groups of people. Bear in mind there was an official KLA investigation which interviewed everybody, but going on in parallel to that Witness 17 asked Mr. Selca to look into what had happened. And he said to you that he had spoken to Shaban Balaj, one source, and he had spoken to Ahmet and Hysen Ukaj another source. Well, they obviously weren't telling him anything about the removal of the body because they had nothing to do with that, so the source must have been Shaban Balaj. And he said in terms he was asked: Where did the information come from in your official report that in all probability Toger moved the body? And he replied: It came from those who were close to her. Well, assuming, as it must be that that was a reference to Sanije Balaj's family and in all probability to the only member of the family he interviewed, Shaban Balaj, then it's plain, isn't it, that the source for that suggestion came from Mete Krasniqi who first said that to Sanije Balaj's family at the second of the two Kanun meetings when he and his brother were threatened with double retribution for the murder. That's the source. And as I said yesterday, all of this ultimately depends on the reliability and credibility of Avni Krasniqi, a man who was plainly lying on oath, and Mete Krasniqi, a man who the Prosecution say is responsible for murder. There is no independent corroboration for that evidence. Six, the orders issued by Mr. Haradinaj after his appointment as zone commander on the 23rd of June. Mr. Re made a great deal of this yesterday at 11045 to 11047, and indeed the suggestion as it was put yesterday is that these orders are evidence of micro-management, but in their closing brief the Prosecution alleges that they are evidence of an attempt to intimidate the civilian population in order to suppress opposition to the joint criminal enterprise. Well, we deal with each of those documents in our brief at paragraphs 910 to 928. Can I just say one or two words about them as a whole? The evidence shows that after his election on the 23rd of June, Mr. Haradinaj issued a number of orders aimed at improving military discipline and organization. He issued the call to arms in the general mobilisation order on the 24th of June, the day after his election; and he issued orders forbidding the consumption of alcohol and the unnecessary firing of weapons; he suspended temporarily political activity; and he passed on the order of the General Staff that after the appointment of Jakup Krasniqi as spokesman, KLA members were not supposed to be giving unauthorised interviews to journalists. Now, out of this the Prosecution seeks to spin a case of Mr. Haradinaj's command of a joint criminal enterprise. It's worth just, again, remembering the chronology. All of these orders were issued after the devastating May offensives and shortly before the summer offensives began in earnest. It is common sense that collective defence of civilian communities required mobilisation. This wasn't an army. These were people, a home guard, faced with the overwhelming might of the Serb military machine in classic asymmetrical warfare. Political activity and uncontrolled contact with journalists were a luxury that could ill be afforded. And in the face of a possible Serb offensive which could come at any time, it's only common sense to say that the consumption of alcohol and the uncontrolled firing of weapons, which after all would provide a target for Serb operations, are a threat to the collective well being of the community. None of this shows either micro-management or any attempt to intimidate; they show a commander who was taking sensible measures to try and ensure a collective defence of the community in the face of attacks which could cost hundreds or even thousands of lives and which were intended to drive the Albanian civilian population out of Kosovo. Seven, interventions. The suggestion that Mr. Haradinaj was party to a joint criminal enterprise to ill-treat collaborators. Mr. Re made no serious attempt to deal with Mr. Haradinaj's response to each and every one of the instances on the evidence where the disappearance or ill-treatment of civilians was reported to him. Skender Kuci, Witness 3, Achilleas Pappas, the investigation conducted by his own military police commander who was appointed on the 25th of July into the disappearance and death of Sanije Balaj and the disappearance of Nurije and Istref Krasniqi. All of these instances, are they all a sham? And what about the canal? This afternoon Mr. Re suggested to you that there were only two individuals, presumably he means leaving aside the unidentified remains, only two individuals who don't fit the profile. What profile one might ask? Because in each and every instance, and you'll read it in their brief, the Prosecution tries any possible means to suggest that someone might be a target for the KLA. Essentially anybody who's not a member of the KLA, says the Prosecution, is a target. And they don't say, Well, we can't fit Afrim Sylejmani or Melush Meha into that pattern, but you the Trial Chamber should be sure they were murdered by the KLA pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise because they were found next to Kujtim Imeraj. And Kujtim Imeraj, says Mr. Re, well, he was plainly abducted and murdered by the KLA. But the Trial Chamber has heard the evidence in relation to Kujtim Imeraj and there is nothing to connect the men who abducted him with either the KLA or with Gllogjan. The witness concerned was asked in terms whether anything about these men who were all in civilian clothes suggested that they were members of the KLA or organization or had insignia or said or did anything that would give such an indication, and the answer was no. But all of that requires a degree of penetration that the Prosecution would prefer that the Trial Chamber did not conduct. And of course there's no serious attempt to deal with Idriz Hoti who was a KLA supporter and on his way to join the KLA when he was last seen in an area where fighting was taking place, or Tush and Illira Frrokaj who Mr. Re suggests were abducted at a check-point in Gllogjan and there's just simply no evidence for that all and no evidence for any motive either. In each of these respects, we submit to the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution adopts classically contrived interpretations of the evidence in order to come to a classically contrived interpretation of the overall picture. The Trial Chamber raised a little earlier on today the question of character. I want, if I may, just to conclude with very brief reference to the two character references which are filed with our brief in annex 2. Klaus Reinhardt, the former commander of KFOR forces in Kosovo was closely involved with Mr. Haradinaj very shortly after the end of the war. He describes him as a leader who was dedicated to putting an end to ethnic fighting in Kosovo and as the only Kosovar Albanian leader who consistently emphasised the importance of recognition -- of reconciliation with Serb minority groups. Soren Jessen-Petersen was the special representative of the United Nations Secretary-General in Kosovo during Mr. Haradinaj's tenure as prime minister. He also describes the importance which Mr. Haradinaj attached to initiatives aimed at integrating and protecting the rights of the Serb civilian minority in Kosovo and the effort which he put into the establishment of a truly multi-ethnic society. Both men are of course giving their assessments of Mr. Haradinaj after the end of the war, albeit in Mr. Reinhardt's case immediately after the end of the war. But even so, the person they describe is a leader with a demonstrated commitment to protecting vulnerable civilians and not attacking them. These are independent assessments by two very experienced members of the international community, and in our submission their views, which they have in the past expressed in documents filed in support of provisional release applications should carry considerable weight with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- address the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I adopt the remarks made by my colleague with regard to the factual matters and I will not repeat them now. I find myself today in the similar if not exact position of yesterday when I raised with this Chamber the terrible concern I have with regard to the issue of rumour because an examination of the record, be it careful or even be it cursory, establishes without a doubt that there was no sighting of Idriz Balaj or Togeri and we do not in any fashion whatsoever suggest that Idriz Balaj during this period of time was not known by that name was ever seen at the canal. There is no evidence at all -- and actually affirmative evidence that certainly after the assault on Gllogjan Idriz Balaj was never seen at Jabllanice. There is evidence that he was seen in a number of different places, which makes very good sense considering what his function was. Does anybody in this room not believe that he was the commander of the Black Eagles, a special intervention unit, who had a specific purpose within the context of what was occurring in that area during the summer of 1998? As a commander, it makes sense, especially when we're dealing with the size of not only his unit but also the types of interventions that they had to engage in that he would be seen and move about because that was his function, to move about. In the remarks made today by Mr. Re, he once again suggests in his argument a proof which is based upon a conclusion that is not supported by the evidence. He told you today you have to consider Balaj's modus operandi, and then the facts as he relies upon all require one very simple proof, which is that the individual who was involved in these activities was Idriz Balaj. I invite you to review the video of the swearing in at Baran which is his seventh point and really the only point in here in his argument that suggests that you will be able to identify Toger as being at the swearing-in video at Baran. For a moment I take a bit of liberty. I do not consider this testimony, but I have gone through that video. I know many others on this side of the room have searched that video looking for Idriz Balaj and have not found his likeness. Perhaps you will. Mr. Re says that I failed to put to Witness 4 that Toger did not introduce himself to Witness 4 as Toger, and he's right because Witness 4 never testified that anybody introduced themselves to him. As a matter of fact, as I discussed with you yesterday, Witness 4's understanding of the name of Toger was something that came in the absence of seeing anybody. He did not see the man the soldiers were calling by this name. There is an assumption that is being made here, and the assumption is that nobody ever called somebody by a name that wasn't their own or by a nickname that wasn't theirs, that people did not misuse or use for that matter another's name. And as a matter of fact, we know that is not the case. We know that is not the case specifically with regard to the testimony that we heard from Witness 4 where some other individual, somebody who he knew claimed to be Ramush Haradinaj. And there's also something else here that seems to have been forgotten in the shuffle which is Toger has a particular significance; it means: Lieutenant. So in such a situation is it unreasonable? Is it unfathomable? Is it not probable that one or another of a soldier would call somebody who had higher rank "lieutenant," which would then translate for purposes of our discussion now to Toger. Mr. Re has told you, But they all knew who Toger was even if they didn't know his name, and by process of elimination, there being no other Toger in the zone, much less one matching the description of Idriz Balaj, the only conclusion available on the evidence that Toger is a person who personally committed the crimes, Idriz Balaj. We have moved in this criminal trial to a process of elimination. That is proof beyond a reasonable doubt? We have moved in this trial to suggest much less one matching the description, you gentlemen have no description, none was ever given. What you have is a myth. What you have is a rumour. I will give you a description that exists in the testimony. "Togeri was described as such at the time. Everything that was happening, the worst things that were happening there then were attributed to Togeri, although he may not have been at that site. So there is nothing specific which I have seen with my own eyes, so I'm just asking both Your Honours and the Prosecution to ask me about things which I could have seen with my own eyes." One of Your Honours: "Yes, could you tell us, you said Togeri was described as such, could you tell us by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In all villages rumours were spread that this was Togeri who was the source of this and that, but I cannot confirm anything because I have not seen anything like that. It was being commented like that, but as to the reality, I don't know. It's true that he was more dynamic and he was more serious in his tone. That is probably why people reached that conclusion. There was a lot of rumours going around that he did this and he did that, but I have not seen anything and I do not know exactly anything of this sort so I cannot confirm it." One of Your Honours: "You said he was more dynamic. Could you tell us what you exactly mean by that? "He was more enthusiastic. He was cool, but he was by nature and his looks like that. Here is a description. The image that people were talking about, it was something which they had created in their own heads. I don't know how." There's no evidence that was presented that the Black Eagles went into any villages, targeted anybody, no evidence was presented that the Black Eagles committed any crimes. No proof upon which you can rely. And ultimately here we have one of the most dangerous forms of argument that I think exists, which is: We've heard an awful lot about people thinking he's a bad man and he did bad things, and so, you know, what? Based on that you ought to convict him. But that's the reason why we have criminal trials. That's the reason why the burden of proof exists, so that people are not subjected to these particular slings and arrows and specifically so Idriz Balaj who it has been acknowledged was a commander and a fierce warrior and a good soldier fighting for the freedom of his country will not be convicted on rumour and speculation. Because when you examine the evidence, Your Honours, the identifications suggested by the Prosecution upon which you should rely are unsafe or non-existent. I think you well know where Idriz Balaj has been since 2002. He suffered, and survived, an assassination attempt. His wife lost her leg, they lost a child. As you know, he came here from being in prison in Kosovo and he continues to serve that sentence. I've never been in quite this particular position in defending a man where -- and I know I've done a lot of jury trials and jury trials are really quite different than the trial that we have here. But I have never been confronted with so much rumour, so much speculation, and so little proof upon which the Prosecution relies in order to obtain a conviction. They have failed to prove their case against Idriz Balaj; an examination of this record will show that. I have no doubt that you will go through the record with a fine-tooth comb. I have no doubt that you will subject it to great scrutiny, and I have no doubt that you will not fall victim to the Prosecution's suggestions that you can find a man guilty based on assumption, conjecture, or speculation, and most assuredly not based upon the fact that they're bad rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we listened carefully to Mr. Re this afternoon. We believe the points we made yesterday stand intact today. We have nothing to add and we stand upon the case we have submitted to you. On the issue of character, Lahi Brahimaj is a war hero not a war criminal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to have a break before we put further questions to the parties, but there's one matter, Mr. Emmerson. You said the Chamber raised the issue of character. As a matter of fact, I did not raise the issue of character, I raised the issue of aggravating or mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour did mention that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand from your answer that the two character, as you call them, references that you want to rely upon them in the context of sentencing if it ever comes to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we made it reasonably clear in the brief that that is the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you say, I reserve the right to respond to your oral submissions and then we rely, whether you explicitly would have to do that or whether it's implied. Then I understand this to be then invoking more or less post-indictment attitude and conduct which would serve as a mitigating circumstance?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As I indicated, both of these witnesses were witnesses who dealt with Mr. Haradinaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to characterize more or less in the framework of our case law. And for you, Mr. Harvey, that's of course a bit different. Where you talked about character, you characterized the person as a whole and not -- and as a matter of fact what you did is you referred to the time-frame in which the crimes as alleged are placed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did so because I believe that the Trial Chamber is already in full possession of all of the information you need concerning my client's character and conduct throughout these proceedings, his respect for this Tribunal, and his compliance with all of its requirements. And I think you know his family background. I don't think that there's anything that I can add to the sum of your knowledge in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now clear on the record what type of mitigating circumstances because I understand that your reference to the two letters to be invoking those mitigating circumstances. Now it's clear for me as well what in I would say a one-liner was comprised as mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I've always tried to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so that we might make best possible use of the break if there are any matters on which it would be helpful for us to conduct research in respect of questions that the Trial Chamber might put to us and any message that might be sent out through the registry in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think so as a matter of fact. We'll then use the next 20 minutes to see whether the questions we had in mind need to be completed or adjusted. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Chamber -- the Judges will put questions to the parties, I'd like to deal with two procedural matters, the one that could not possibly affect the trial but nevertheless ready as ready, that is a direction to the registrar to make certain sections of Fadil Fazliu's evidence public. I think I raised the matter last Monday. The Chamber has received submissions by all parties on the sections of Fadil Fazliu's evidence which were heard in private session and which the Chamber proposes to make public. The only party to provide any objection was the Prosecution, which submitted that certain sections if made public could identify protected witnesses or reveal contact between the Prosecution and intended witnesses. The Chamber has reviewed the submissions of the Prosecution and agrees not to make those sections public. The registrar is therefore ordered to make public the following sections of the transcript: Page 7415, line 6, to page 7425, line 13; page 7427, line 24, to page 7445, line 15; page 7452, line 19, to page 7456, line 2; page 7456, line 5, to page 7471, line 16; page 7471, line 20, to page 7473, line 5 -- 6, line 6; page 7484, line 7, to page 7486, line 4; page 7486, line 23, to page 7487, line 23; page 7488, line 16, to page 7499, line 24; page 7509, line 15, to page 7513, line 4; page 7515, line 12, to page 7531, line 8. This concludes the order to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second matter I would like to raise is the following. The Balaj Defence filed on the 30th of October Idriz Balaj's citation of prosecutoral violation of ethical code of conduct and requests for evidentiary hearing regarding interview of Carla del Ponte. The Brahimaj Defence joined in this request. The Chamber denies the request and a written version with full reasons will follow soon. As far as the Chamber is aware, there is no motion or request pending at this moment which could possibly have any impact on the judgement that the Chamber will deliver. If the Chamber oversees something, then of course it would like to know. Nothing there --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There may be one matter I think at one point we had asked for an exhibit number for a particular document and I need to go back and double-check to make sure, but I'll double-check and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think it will affect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we need just an exhibit number, then of course that's a technicality --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it could have no impact on decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Re, earlier today Mr. Emmerson referred to an exhibit for which he said there was no official translation uploaded into e-court. Now, I do not think that any of the Defence counsel where they said that they had their own translation of this document, I take it you shared that with the others, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely sure whether we have shared it with the others, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you would do that, I take it, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because of course in e-court, Mr. Re, we have no official translation, there's even no translation at all in e-court at this moment, so I tried to verify it to follow the words of Mr. Emmerson, but I had difficulties in -- Mr. Emmerson said there was a provisional translation -- I take it that that is something that the official translation will be uploaded. May I also take it that the Defence is not in any way prejudiced by looking at that translation once it is uploaded? And that's of course the translation the Chamber will then look at. That's first. Of course if there's any problem with the translation, which is a technical matter, it's not a matter of opinion, but -- well, it's a matter of providing the Chamber with an official translation which is not challenged by any of the parties. Such a challenge, which again could have no impact on the decision -- of course a wrong translation could, but challenging the translation as such could not have an impact on any determination the Chamber will have to make. So I take it that the parties would agree that they will be informed once the official translation is uploaded; and if there's any problem with the translation as such, which is a linguistical, technical matter, that the Chamber will deal with that and hear, if there are any, hear the complaints and then of course the usual way will be followed, that is that CLSS, of course, will comment on it, and that we finally will all be provided with a translation which serves us. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour asked about outstanding motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They're not strictly speaking an outstanding motion. The Trial Chamber issued a request on the 5th of December to the Prosecution in respect of the Swiss conviction of Avni Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've made certain submissions in our closing brief about the approach the Trial Chamber should take in relation to assessing Avni Krasniqi's credibility as regards that conviction. Those submissions obviously stand unless or until the Swiss judgement is obtained, and if and when it is obtained, it may be that further submissions at that stage would need to be made upon it; but at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that then it could be brief written submissions rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we cannot take action on it at this moment further. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite my fellow Judges to put questions to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to pose two questions to the Prosecution. They have to do first with the definition of a collaborator; and then second with the alleged rape which is referred to in the last two counts of the indictment. As to the first one, what is the Prosecution's understanding of the term "collaborator" as used throughout the indictment? Do you consider these persons as civilians or as taking part in hostilities? That is the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution's view is that the collaborators as defined and as our case has unfolded, everyone within what is understood to be within that meaning was a civilian. I appreciate the distinction under the Geneva Conventions and the treatment, but the people who the KLA targeted as perceived collaborators were civilians who were taking no active part in hostilities, they were just simply not members of the military of the opposing side. They were civilians perceived not to be supporting the KLA. So in that sense, it's a wider definition that we've used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That had been raised by Mr. Emmerson and I would have expected to hear a response to that and so this is now clear. And as to this rape, you spoke of patterns of attacks against a civilian population. Do you consider the alleged rape part of such an attack? Could you respond, please, both in terms of crimes against humanity and war crimes, apart from the geographical and temporal proximity to armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, absolutely yes. The crimes against civilians as part of the crimes against humanity, all of course committed against a civilian population, were many and varied and numerous, torture, cruel treatment, inhumane acts, forcible displacement, and rape. It falls within the pattern of attacks against civilians who the KLA or members of the joint criminal enterprise were targeting, were in their target group as part of the civilian population. The rape is just yet another crime committed in the context of the war against civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have I answered your question? I'm not quite sure if I'm going where you want me to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I have one follow-up question to a question put to you by Judge Hoepfel. I'm referring to Counts 21 and 22, Rade Popadic. I leave a part at this moment, and that seems to be a matter which is in dispute, whether Rade Popadic was killed in a combat or combat-like activity, at least in an exchange of fire or at least firing at the car when he was still in it or still driving, or that seems to be the Prosecution's case that he was killed not when stopped or abducted, we do not know much about that, but at least that he was as the indictment says he was subsequently killed while in KLA custody, that means that he was taken into custody. Now, could you perhaps expand on your -- was he -- for the -- let's just for argument sake first limit ourselves to a scenario where the car he was driving in was shot at or at least was stopped prior to the abduction by members of the KLA. Was he at that moment, was he a collaborator? Was he a -- was he a civilian? Was he -- could you expand on his situation during this first part of the episode in your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We put our case in relation to Rade Popadic as an attack -- as part of an attack against a civilian population if he were tortured and murdered after his capture or his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you now to limit yourself first to that first part of the episode. I might put questions to you on the follow-up as alleged by the Prosecution. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But that's our case. We don't say he was a collaborator. He was a member of the Serbian forces. He was a member of the PJP on active duty. He was carrying food from Gjakove to the base in Junik, and disappeared en route --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And he was clearly a member of the opposing force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He wasn't a collaborator, no. For the purposes of what happened to him en route as a combatant of course he was a legitimate target of an attack by the opposing force such as the KLA, but he wasn't -- wasn't legitimate to murder or mistreating after capture. And to put it on a dual basis after capture, he was a civilian within the broader definition of a civilian under Article 5 or alternatively simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that -- you are saying that an attack against a civilian population may hit non-civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The argument we've put is best -- yes -- well, it's best put out in the response the Prosecution has filed in the Mrksic appeal where we have appealed against the finding in relation to the Vukovar Hospital about who was a civilian for the purposes of an attack on a civilian population, and our argument is the Trial Chamber was wrong in law and someone who is hors de combat may if they are tied up in the attack for the purposes of Article 5 be treated as a civilian. And our submission is Rade Popadic falls squarely within the definition of the argument within Mrksic. We're saying Mrksic is wrong, but if the Trial Chamber takes -- follows the same line as the Mrksic Trial Chamber does, you'll -- you would have to accept the alternative argument of it being a breach of the laws and conventions of war under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the language of abduction is one as if it would be something illegal. Now, the, as you called it, the abduction of Popadic, you could also -- could you say he was taken prisoner of war in this armed conflict belonging to the armed forces of the opposite ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We put the case that he was a member of the armed -- the opposing armed forces, but once taken prisoner -- I mean, it's described I think more colloquially as an abduction, but once he's captured and taken and imprisoned, clearly all the conventions and the laws of war of the Geneva Conventions applied to his captivity, and our case is they weren't. But I mean we say for the present purposes he should be treated as a civilian under Article 5 as he was at that point hors de combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 26 of the indictment and I'm looking at the common criminal purpose with the consolidated total control and then by several crimes mentioned, that is, mistreatment of several categories of civilians and other civilians who were or were perceived to have been collaborators with the Serbian forces or otherwise not supporting the KLA and it also involved the commission of crimes against humanity. So you would say murder of a prisoner of war would fall within these categories?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It certainly falls within the next line which says: "The JCE included the establishment and operation of KLA detention facilities and the mistreatment of detained persons at these facilities, including at the KLA's headquarters at Jabllanice and Gllogjan and the Black Eagles headquarters." So yes, if someone has been captured and mistreated and murdered, it certainly falls well within the purpose of the common criminal purpose as pleaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it's limited to the Gllogjan and the Jabllanice detention facilities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says "included." It's open to the Trial Chamber to find that they were within the KLA's or members of the joint criminal enterprise's captive -- custody at the time of murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. I have another question and I would rather -- it relates to the KLA/FARK issue, and perhaps I best put the question in the context of an example. It's the Prosecution's case that the Frrokajs were abducted and killed late in August. Now, in that period of time the evidence suggests that Tahir Zemaj had taken over command, overall command of the area. Would that have any consequences, whereas as it is understood by Mr. Emmerson that you exclude FARK soldiers and FARK officers from participating in the joint criminal enterprise and that the KLA command was separate from FARK command. Now, in that situation - and I'm now focusing on the Frrokaj issue, Tahir Zemaj being appointed as an overall commander from what I understand including all the KLA armed forces, would this have any consequences for KLA being alleged to have abducted and being responsible for killing the Frrokajs?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not at all. The FARK wasn't part of this joint criminal enterprise or the common criminal purpose. The evidence of Witness 17 is quite clear on this purpose -- on this point about their reluctance to have anything to do with it and the fact that they wanted to impose military discipline on those particular forces went to a whole range of things through the way that it was organized to the salutes that were employed, a fist versus a normal military salute. It's not -- FARK plays no part in it. Witness 17's evidence is quite clear about the complaints made at the time of people within the -- of the KLA behaviour to Tahir Zemaj. The whole thing about the meeting at Prapaqan and the remark about the fish getting fat in the lake. But most importantly the evidence establishes that Gllogjan was firmly in the control of Ramush Haradinaj at the time, and that's where we say we've proved the Frrokajs disappeared from, as we -- as I argued earlier. There were check-points in and out. The only way in and out is through the check-points or alternatively down the road leading to the lake. So it was an area under KLA, that is, Ramush Haradinaj's command and control at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, would you say that taking over the overall command would not include, at least formally, the areas which were under Ramush Haradinaj's command? Because isn't it true that Tahir Zemaj had taken over the command from Haradinaj or exercised the command, at least that's what some of the documents seem to suggest, that exercised that command prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Our case has been, and in my submission the evidence establishes that there was a parallel command existing at all relevant times after the FARK arrived and our argument is that although Haradinaj handed over "control" to Tahir Zemaj for that period, it was in effect a political exercise which did not last and was not intended to last and FARK shortly after left the zone for reasons which we've set out in our brief. They were not part of the joint criminal enterprise. The formal command did not, if you put Tahir Zemaj in the top of it even for several weeks in August, did not need to play any part in the common criminal purpose. It was not his area. Where the Frrokajs disappeared was well within Ramush Haradinaj's geographical area of control and command, next to Idriz Balaj's Black Eagles' territory or training-ground under their control. The evidence is quite clear on the dispute between FARK and Idriz Balaj with personal confrontations between Tahir Zemaj and Witness 17. So in our submission it makes no difference whatever the "formal" position of Tahir Zemaj was at the time, if he was not part of this more horizontal, as Mr. Emmerson put it, joint criminal enterprise then existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say it was handing over de jure the command but not de facto?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions to you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: One question for the Prosecution or invitation to elaborate a little bit more. Of course this is a case on joint criminal enterprise, and I have listened to what you have said about the necessity for the Trial Chamber to view the evidence in context as a whole and the similarities that you have dwelled upon. If you -- if one approaches the evidence on the facts known, the more individual facts to each count in the indictment, there are several categories: There are some of the counts where we had evidence of more concrete character; there are a category where you had evidence on abduction at different time span before the recovery of the bodies or the remains; and there are a category, leaving the unidentified remains aside, of identified bodies where we have nothing I think apart from the fact or the information that these disappeared at a certain time and then were recovered from the Lake Radoniq canal. Can you explore or expand a little bit more on why, also in that category, those counts covering that category, the Trial Chamber should find that beyond reasonable doubt the accused should be found guilty for those categories. I do understand that the JCE comes into the picture and the location -- recovery at the canal is important. I wonder if you could expand a little bit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To find the accused participated in the joint criminal enterprise and other members of the KLA shared that common criminal purpose, you don't -- the Trial Chamber doesn't need to make a finding in relation to each and every body. We of course cannot exclude that it is possible -- they -- there could be a possibility that -- I'll put it another way around. The Prosecution case is that everybody there is either there as a direct result of the joint criminal enterprise or is a natural and foreseeable consequence of what was going on. And I say that in the sense of the climate of impunity that was allowed to exist within the zone, the degree of control over the zone imposed by Ramush Haradinaj and the KLA, the fact that the canal was firmly on all reliable evidence within KLA and, more specifically, the control of those controlled by Haradinaj at the time, all entrances, all exits into the canal were basically controlled by the KLA. You've heard evidence about the check-points. The only way the bodies could have got in there was either via the Black Eagles training-ground or through KLA-controlled check-points in Gllogjan and down the only access road which took them into the canal itself. As I mentioned earlier in my submissions, if you look at the canal itself as a natural mass grave site and if you look at the length of the canal and if you look at the way -- and we described in our brief the way that the bodies were intermingled, the people who were kidnapped basically in the same order or disappeared one after the other, the classical one of course is Sanije Balaj on top of the bodies of Witness 4's mother and sister. If you put those things together it leads in our submission to one conclusion, that there was only one group of people and that was the group of people who controlled that area who was, A, letting the bodies go in; and B, putting them in. It was well-known at the time amongst those living that there was something going on at the canal. I mean, the fish getting fat comment, the thing about going -- being taken to Gllogjan, Mr. Guy-Smith said it, there were rumours, but in this case it's one where the rumours actually had some real meat to it. So if you look at -- and you've got to look at each of the bodies individually but then put them together, where they were found in the canyon, who controlled access to it, who controlled the whole area, the similarities in death, the gun-shot wounds, the fact that it -- you could conclude beyond reasonable doubt that some of them had been probably executed at the wall, that's consistent with the execution bodies found under the bullet-holes. Once you do that with each and every body and put them all together, the Trial Chamber can find beyond reasonable doubt, it can exclude any other hypothesis, any reasonable hypothesis other than that they were all put there either directly or as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the enterprise that allowed this to occur. Even if you look at the number of bodies in an area that size, 40 bodies within a geographically small area over a period of some four to five months, an area controlled at the time by the KLA, and the bodies all, except the unidentified ones, fitting within a clear pattern, that is, collaborators, perceived collaborators and Serb civilians. And you put that altogether, the number of the bodies and where they were found, our submission is there is simply no other explanation for what happened. Does that answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has no further questions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If our questions have raised any concerns with the parties or any need to further address us, then of course I would like to hear; but if that's not the case then this concludes this trial. The Chamber will consider everything that has been put before it. The Chamber will consider the evidence that was presented. The Chamber will consider all the submissions made by the parties, and then it's up to the Chamber to prepare, write, the judgement which will be delivered in due course. Now, I do understand that the parties would like to know when that will be. The Chamber cannot give any date nor will it limit itself to certain periods, especially if this would assist you. The parties may be aware that a Pre-Trial Conference has been set in the Gotovina case, which as far as I can see I will preside over for the 10th of March. The case to -- the trial to start on the 11th of March. If you have looked carefully at the scheduling, you will also see that the case will not immediately continue after the 14th of March, so that would leave some time. The Chamber does not commit itself that it will not deliver a judgement before the 10th of March, neither does the Chamber promise or raise the expectation that a judgement will be delivered before the 10th of March. I'm -- I would like to express further that the parties have certainly assisted the Chamber in their professional performance during this trial. They certainly have assisted the Chamber far better than I assisted the parties half a minute ago about when they could expect the judgement in this case. It may be clear that it is important for a Chamber to have the professional and committed assistance of counsel because it assists the Chamber in making the determinations it has to make. We stand adjourned sine die and the next thing the Chamber expects to deliver is a Scheduling Order for the delivery of the judgement unless anything comes in between.
